name: AI Query Optimisation
title: AI Query Optimisation
answer: AI query optimisation covers the systems that decide how a database executes a query, and the machine learning methods now used to make those decisions. A query optimiser picks join orders, access paths and index usage, and the newer work applies learned models to cost estimation, index recommendation and automatic tuning of settings. The appeal is better plans on workloads that defeat hand written rules, and the risk is that a learned choice is hard to explain when it goes wrong. This sits inside the broader field of AI and SQL, alongside the assistants and agents that write and run queries.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the database engine itself, most often PostgreSQL, MySQL or a cloud warehouse, with the optimiser either extended in place or shadowed by an external planner. Training and evaluation need query logs, schema statistics and execution traces, which are collected from production or from benchmark workloads replayed on test instances. Model Context Protocol servers are one route to that data, and this site tracks 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses out of 2526 active servers. Every page on this site is itself built from a PostgreSQL database, so the same statistics and plan inspection tools are close at hand.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start from the query workload and the plans the existing optimiser produces, then label those plans with real execution times rather than estimated costs. Learned components range from cardinality estimators trained on query fragments to reinforcement learning agents that pick join orders, and index advisors that score candidate index sets against sampled queries. Evaluation compares the learned planner against the baseline on latency, throughput and plan stability, with regression tests for queries where the model does worse. Because a plan is only as good as its cost model, teams keep a fallback to the rule based optimiser and log when the two disagree.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main governance question is explainability, since a learned plan that performs badly is difficult to justify to the person who owns the query. Teams keep the training data, model version and the plan chosen for each query so a decision can be reconstructed later, and they set limits on what the optimiser may change without review. Access to query logs and execution traces is restricted because those records often contain sensitive values, and index recommendations can alter write performance across an entire database. Nothing here is legal advice, and any change to a production database should follow the organisation's own change control.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward optimisers that adapt to a workload as it shifts, rather than being retrained in occasional batches. That means tighter feedback loops from execution results back into the cost model, and more use of language models to translate a stated intent into a candidate plan for a human to approve. The open problems are stability, so a learned planner does not oscillate between plans, and portability, so a model trained on one schema is useful on another. Expect the rule based optimiser to remain as a reference point for some time, with learned components layered on top rather than replacing it outright.
